meta.name: Sigil Core — Structural Checks
meta.author: NOMARK <hello@sigilsec.ai>
meta.description: Rules implemented in the scanner engine rather than as regexes: shipped Python bytecode compared against its source, executables disguised under document names, archive contents, whitespace padding that hides instructions, declared-versus-used privilege, and npm lifecycle scripts or launchers proven unable to act on the installing machine. This pack documents them; the detection lives in cli/src/scanner/{bytecode,artifacts,padding,lpriv,lifecycle}.rs.

engine_rules.description: Python bytecode shipped that could not be matched to its source (.pyc / .pyo / __pycache__)
engine_rules.remediation: Bytecode runs but cannot be reviewed, and this file could not be shown to be the .py beside it: it has no source-size field (Python 2 / 3.0-3.2), uses an unchecked hash (PEP 552) that Python never verifies, its source is missing or too large to compare, or it diverges from the source (see ARTIFACT-002/003 on the same files). Delete every __pycache__/ directory and .pyc/.pyo file from the skill or package, add them to the ignore list used when publishing, and review only the source. If the author insists on shipping bytecode, ask why; a skill has no reason to.
references: OWASP Agentic Top 10 — Agentic Supply Chain

engine_rules.description: Bytecode runs instead of the reviewed source (unchecked or loadable pyc that is not the .py, or sourceless importable .pyc)
engine_rules.remediation: Python will load this bytecode instead of compiling the .py a reviewer reads: an unchecked hash-based pyc (PEP 552) is never compared with its source, a pyc whose checked hash or recorded mtime and size match the source is loaded as-is, and a .pyc beside a package with no .py is imported directly - and this one's header hash, or its constants (URLs, identifiers the source never mentions), show it was compiled from other code. Treat the skill as backdoored: do not install or run it, disassemble the .pyc (python -m dis, or decompyle3 in an isolated VM) to see what it does, and report the publisher.
references: OWASP Agentic Top 10 — Agentic Supply Chain

engine_rules.description: Bytecode compiled from different source than shipped
engine_rules.remediation: The pyc header or its constants disagree with the shipped .py: a recorded source size no line-ending conversion explains, a checked hash that does not match, bytecode with no source at all, or URL constants or three or more identifiers the source never mentions. Python recompiles a stale timestamp pyc rather than load it, but the file still proves the author ran different code than they published. Read the extracted constants in the finding's derived units, remove the bytecode, and do not trust the package until the difference is explained.

engine_rules.description: Executable disguised under a document, text, image or source-code name
engine_rules.remediation: The file's magic bytes say ELF, PE, Mach-O, Java class or WebAssembly while its name claims a document, image, text or source file (a helper.py or run.sh that is machine code runs as a program when invoked as ./helper.py). There is no packaging reason for that; it exists to get past a reviewer who trusts extensions. Do not run the skill. Identify the binary (file, sha256 against a malware database) in an isolated environment, and check the skill's scripts for whatever renames, chmods or executes it.
references: OWASP Agentic Top 10 — Unexpected Code Execution

engine_rules.description: Archive or script disguised under a document, text, image or source-code name
engine_rules.remediation: The file is an archive (zip, gzip, tar, 7z, rar...) while its name claims a document, image, text or source file - python app.py runs the __main__.py inside a zip named app.py - or a #! script named as a document or image. Sigil still opens zip and tar contents and scans them; review those findings, then ask why the file is named as something else. Office formats that are zips by design (docx, xlsx, pptx, epub) are not reported here.

engine_rules.description: Native executable in a hidden file or directory
engine_rules.remediation: A compiled executable sits under a dot-file or dot-directory, out of sight in a normal listing. Find what references it (grep the skill for the path), confirm where it came from, and remove it unless it is a documented, reproducible build of source that ships alongside it.

engine_rules.description: Archive shipped in the tree (contents inspected)
engine_rules.remediation: Observation only: the archive was opened in memory and its text members were scanned like any other file (findings inside it carry paths such as bundle.zip!/path). Check whether the archive is needed at all; a skill that unpacks an archive at run time ships code a reviewer has to open by hand.

engine_rules.description: Archive could not be fully inspected
engine_rules.remediation: Part of the archive was not scanned: it is corrupt, uses a format Sigil does not open (7z, rar, bzip2, xz), nests archives more than two levels deep, or exceeded the member, size or total-bytes caps. Unpack it in a sandbox and scan the result with sigil scan before trusting it.

engine_rules.description: Encrypted (password-protected) archive member
engine_rules.remediation: Encrypting an archive member defeats every scanner, which is why malware droppers do it. A skill has no reason to ship content its reviewer cannot read; reject it unless the password and the decrypted content are provided and reviewed.

engine_rules.description: Archive member escapes the extraction root (zip-slip)
engine_rules.remediation: A member path contains '..' or is absolute, or a link points outside the archive, so an extractor that trusts member names writes outside its target directory (overwriting shell profiles, SSH config, agent settings). Do not extract the archive with a tool that does not refuse such entries; treat the archive as hostile.

engine_rules.description: Executable or bytecode inside an archive
engine_rules.remediation: An archive in the tree carries compiled code (ELF/PE/Mach-O/class/WASM/pyc). Packing a binary inside an archive adds a step between the reviewer and the code. Identify each binary, confirm it is reproducible from source that ships with the skill, or remove it. Java archives (.jar/.war) are not reported here: PROV-002 covers them.

engine_rules.description: Python bytecode cache that matches its shipped source
engine_rules.remediation: Observation only: CPython writes __pycache__/<module>.cpython-3xx.pyc beside a script the first time it runs, so an installed skill that has been used once has these. Each file's header (recorded source size, or a checked hash) agrees with the .py beside it and its string constants name nothing the source does not, so it is the compiled source. Delete the __pycache__ directories before publishing a skill; a reviewer should not have to take bytecode on trust.

engine_rules.description: Whitespace padding hides instruction-like text
engine_rules.remediation: A run of blank lines, spaces or invisible Unicode fillers pushes text below the fold or past the right edge of an editor, and what sits there reads as an instruction (override, secrecy, exfiltration, a command). The model reads it even though a reviewer scrolling the file will not. Open the file at the reported line, read the hidden text, and reject the skill if it instructs the agent to do something the visible description does not.
references: OWASP Agentic Top 10 — Agent Goal Hijack

engine_rules.description: Whitespace padding pushes text out of view
engine_rules.remediation: Text follows a padding run large enough to hide it in a normal view of the file. It did not match instruction wording, so this is suspicious rather than conclusive: read the text at the reported line and remove the padding.

engine_rules.description: Large whitespace padding with nothing after it
engine_rules.remediation: Observation only: a large run of padding with no meaningful text after it hides nothing today, but it is the shape used to hide text and is not something a hand-written instruction file contains. Trim it.

engine_rules.description: Skill scripts use capabilities its declaration does not cover
engine_rules.remediation: The skill declares allowed-tools or permissions, and its own scripts were seen using something that declaration does not include (shell, network, credential or environment access, file writes). Either the declaration understates what the skill does, which misleads the reviewer who approved it, or the scripts do something the author did not intend. Compare the evidence listed in the finding with the declaration and the description.
references: OWASP Agentic Top 10 — Identity and Privilege Abuse

engine_rules.description: Wildcard permission grant in a skill declaration
engine_rules.remediation: A permissions or allowed-tools entry of '*', 'all', 'full' or 'any' removes the least-privilege boundary. Replace it with the specific capabilities the skill needs. (SKILL-008 reports the JSON and single-line forms at High; this covers the rest.)

engine_rules.description: Declared permission no script uses
engine_rules.remediation: Observation only: the skill asks for a capability none of its scripts were seen using. Remove it, so an approval covers exactly what the skill does and a later update cannot start using it silently.

engine_rules.description: Part of the target was not fully inspected (unreadable file or directory, oversized file scanned only at its ends, file over the 512 MB limit)
engine_rules.remediation: Nothing was found in what could not be read, which is not the same as nothing being there. Check the named file by hand, or make it readable and re-scan. In CI or an install gate, run with --fail-on-incomplete (or fail_on_incomplete: true in the scan policy) so an incomplete scan never passes.
references: OWASP Agentic Top 10 — Agentic Supply Chain

engine_rules.description: Scan budget exhausted: the file was not fully analysed
engine_rules.remediation: The decode worklist for this file did not finish within SIGIL_FILE_BUDGET_SECS (default 30 s). Content built to exhaust a scanner is itself suspicious: review the file by hand, or re-scan with a larger budget (SIGIL_FILE_BUDGET_SECS=0 disables the bound). Use --fail-on-incomplete to fail the scan on it.

engine_rules.description: NUL bytes inside an otherwise ordinary text file
engine_rules.remediation: Text files do not contain NUL bytes. Many scanners treat any NUL as 'binary' and skip the whole file, while bash drops NULs and runs the rest, so a stray NUL is a cheap way to hide a script or an instruction file. Sigil removes them and scans the text; read the file at the reported line and reject it unless the NULs have an innocent explanation (a test fixture for a parser, say).
references: OWASP Agentic Top 10 — Agentic Supply Chain

engine_rules.description: npm lifecycle script that only runs an inert local script
engine_rules.remediation: A preinstall or postinstall that is exactly node <script inside the package>, where that script and the local scripts it requires (two levels deep) are short, plain ASCII, load nothing but os, path, url, util and relative JSON, use process only for exit, argv, platform, arch, version, stdout, stderr and cwd, and use no network, filesystem, child-process, environment, eval, Function or reflection API. It still runs on every npm install, so it is Medium rather than Low: read the script, confirm it only checks the platform or prints a message, and re-read it whenever the package updates. Any change that adds a capability returns the finding to INSTALL-003 (Critical).

engine_rules.description: npm lifecycle script that only enforces a package manager (only-allow)
engine_rules.remediation: The lifecycle command is exactly npx only-allow pnpm (or yarn, npm, bun), a guard that stops installs with the wrong package manager. It is Low because the command is fixed and only-allow is fetched from the public registry: the package does not declare, bundle, override or ship its own only-allow, and no node_modules or binding.gyp sits beside the manifest. Anything added to the command (&&, ;, a version pin, another tool) returns the finding to INSTALL-003 (Critical).

engine_rules.description: npm prepare/prepublish script that only builds the package
engine_rules.remediation: Every command this prepare or prepublish script runs, following npm run chains three levels deep and the pre/post scripts npm runs around them, is a build step: tsc (flags or a tsconfig .json only), husky, chmod +x, shx mkdir/cp/rm or rimraf on package-relative paths, true or exit 0. The tools come from the public registry (no git, file, tarball or alias spec, no bundling, override, lockfile redirect or shipped node_modules). prepare runs on git-dependency and checkout installs, not registry installs; a script that adds any other command returns the finding to INSTALL-004 (Medium).

engine_rules.description: Launcher installs its own platform-specific package at run time
engine_rules.remediation: A bin script runs execSync(`npm install ${X}@${Y}`) where X is proven to be the package's own name joined with os.platform()/process.platform and os.arch()/process.arch, Y its own version, both read from its own package.json through single-assignment constants, and the manifest lists at least two such platform packages at that version as optionalDependencies. The only flags are ones that do not change what is installed or where from, and the options object sets no env, shell or uid. This is the platform-binary launcher pattern; it still installs code at run time, so confirm the platform packages are published by the same owner. Any other command shape returns the finding to CODE-014 (High).
